text.p: International trade in caviar would be closely regulated under a German-U.S. proposal to list sturgeons as a species requiring protection, conservation officials said on Friday.

The secretariat of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), saying over-fishing and pollution were threatening stocks, recommended its 138 members adopt the measure in Harare next month.

But the Swiss-based group warned it could mean the end of lucrative sales of caviar at airport duty-free shops because hurried passengers are generally not in a position to obtain CITES export permits or certificates from national authorities.

Three African countries with elephant populations in need of culling (Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe) have also suggested their species be "downlisted" to allow limited trade in tusks, hunting trophies and live animals, according to CITES.
CITES backed the elaborate plan, which would allow elephant exports by the three only to Japan under fixed annual quotas.

Member states will meet in Harare from June 9-20 to discuss 75 proposals involving 89 species covered by CITES, one of the world's first environmental treaties. Amendments require a two-thirds majority but are usually agreed by consensus.

Izgrev Topkov, secretary-general of the CITES secretariat, told a news conference: "This so-called jubilee 10th meeting of the Conference of the Parties is probably going to be the most difficult ever."

Germany and the United States have proposed including five sturgeon species and 18 "look-alike" species often mistaken for caviar-producing fish on CITES appendix II. The classification covers species not necessarily in danger of extinction but which could become so if trade were not strictly regulated.

"There are many more sturgeon-range states along the Danube and so on, but we are speaking really seriously about the Caspian sturgeon region which is the most important commercially-traded," said Topkov, who is Bulgarian.

Previously, under an agreement with the former Soviet Union, caviar was distributed by Moscow under quotas to the other four states bordering the Caspian -- Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan. Only Russia and Iran are members of CITES.

"It would be in the interest of the five countries for the trade to be controlled. Otherwise this is a closed sea and the stocks may finish rather quickly just for illegal and Mafia-type structures to make quick money without taking care about what's going to happen in five years," Topkov said.

"Now with the dissolution, the illegal catch started (to be) absolutely uncontrolled. We are bothered with all of the countries. Admittedly however, the control on the side of the Russian Federation and Iran is probably better..." he added.

In a report to the Harare talks, CITES secretariat backed the proposal, but pointed to difficult enforcement of trade regulations "because it is very easy to smuggle small quantities of caviar that have a very high value".

"There is no doubt that the status of the populations of all sturgeon species gives cause for concern. The main reason is over-fishing, much of it illegally, which is aggravated, particularly in the Caspian Sea, by pollution," it added.

The Russian Federation does not limit the commercial export of caviar but does limit its export by private persons. CITES recommended the staff at Moscow's Cheremetivo airport, "well-trained to detect the caviar in the luggage of passengers", share its detection techniques with other states.
Obdulio Menghi, CITES's scientific coordinator, said: "We intend to protect certain species which produce cavier but we also intend to protect 18 species more for 'look-alike reasons'.
"We have a real problem in conservation of the species."
Appendix II allows international trade of listed species, but a country has to determine that the trade is "not detrimental" to the survival of the species.

A country's designated scientific authority advises on the status of a species and eligibility for trade. Its "management authorities" must issue a permit or certificate for export, re-export, or import for trade in species or their products.
CITES, signed in 1973, covers 39,000 species. Some 800 plant and animal species are on its appendix I of species too severely endangered to be traded with few excpetions.
